---
title: "Installation"
---

juphyter has two halves. The engine that runs your cells is PHP, and the
transport that speaks the Jupyter protocol is a small Python module that runs
inside `ipykernel`. Installing juphyter means putting a kernelspec where Jupyter
looks for one, pointing at both.

A kernelspec belongs to the machine rather than to a project. There is one
`php` kernel per user, whatever directory you installed from, so installing
juphyter once for your user is the usual choice. The engine does not need to
live in a project either: it starts in the document's own directory and walks
up for a `vendor/autoload.php`, so a document anywhere on disk gets a working
PHP kernel.

## Requirements

- **PHP 8.3 or later**, from Homebrew, Herd, or a distribution package. That
  floor matches phibble and phplyr. phiz needs PHP 8.5, so plots are available
  only on a kernel running 8.5 or newer.
- **Composer.**
- **Python 3 with `jupyter` and `ipykernel` 7.0 or later.** The wrapper
  subclasses `ipykernel.kernelbase.Kernel`, which changed in version 7. This
  costs nothing extra in practice: JupyterLab is a Python application, and
  Quarto's jupyter engine requires a Python Jupyter whatever kernel it drives.
- **Quarto**, to render Quarto documents.
- **macOS or Linux.** The kernel interrupts a running cell with POSIX signals,
  which the Windows PHP build does not provide.

`pcntl` is wanted rather than required. Without it the kernel runs and the stop
button does nothing, so `juphyter install` checks the PHP binary it is about to
name and says so rather than refusing to install.

## Install

Copy the whole block:

```bash
# Does the Python that Quarto will use already have Jupyter?
py="$(command -v python3)"
"$py" -c 'import jupyter_client' 2>/dev/null || py=''

# juphyter. It is not on Packagist yet, so Composer reads the repository
# directly, which "no-api" does over git and without a GitHub token.
composer global config repositories.juphyter \
  '{"type":"vcs","url":"https://github.com/phpstats/juphyter","no-api":true}'
composer global require phpstats/juphyter:dev-main

# The juphyter command on PATH.
bin="$(composer global config bin-dir --absolute 2>/dev/null)"
export PATH="$bin:$PATH"
grep -qF "$bin" ~/.zshrc 2>/dev/null \
  || echo "export PATH=\"$bin:\$PATH\"" >> ~/.zshrc

# Jupyter, in a virtual environment, only when that Python has none. Quarto
# picks it up as the python3 on PATH.
if [ -z "$py" ]; then
  python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/juphyter
  ~/.venvs/juphyter/bin/pip install jupyterlab
  export PATH="$HOME/.venvs/juphyter/bin:$PATH"
  grep -qF '.venvs/juphyter/bin' ~/.zshrc 2>/dev/null \
    || echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.venvs/juphyter/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
  py="$HOME/.venvs/juphyter/bin/python"
fi

# The kernelspec, naming that Python and the PHP on PATH.
juphyter install --python "$py"

# Check. It reports what it found and fails if anything is broken.
juphyter doctor
```

On a machine running bash, write `~/.bashrc` in place of `~/.zshrc`.

`juphyter install` prints where the kernelspec went, which Python, PHP, and
engine it recorded, and which Python Quarto appears to use:

```
Installed the juphyter kernel "php" for PHP 8.5.10.
  kernel.json  /Users/you/Library/Jupyter/kernels/php/kernel.json
  python       /Users/you/.venvs/juphyter/bin/python (ipykernel 7.4.0)
  php          /opt/homebrew/bin/php
  engine       /Users/you/.composer/vendor/phpstats/juphyter/bin/juphyter
  quarto       /Users/you/.venvs/juphyter/bin/python (jupyter_client 8.10.0)
```

If `ipykernel` is missing from that interpreter the command writes nothing and
prints the `pip install` line that fixes it. The interpreter it picks is the one
that owns the `jupyter` on your `PATH`, read from that script's shebang, because
that is the environment your Jupyter actually runs in. Use `--python` to name a
different one.

The `quarto` line is a different question from the `python` line above, and the
command reports it rather than acting on it. The line is absent when `quarto` is
not on your `PATH`. When the interpreter Quarto will run has no Jupyter in it,
the line says so and the command prints a warning naming the `PATH` entry that
fixes it:

```
  quarto       /opt/homebrew/opt/python@3.14/bin/python3.14 (no Jupyter)
```

The kernelspec is still written and the command still exits 0, because a kernel
Quarto cannot reach is a working JupyterLab kernel. `quarto check jupyter` is
the authority on which interpreter Quarto chose, and the section below explains
the failure the warning is about.

### Why the kernel is installed against Quarto's Python

Quarto chooses its own Python, independently of the one that installed the
kernel, and the interpreter it chooses is the one that has to have Jupyter,
because Jupyter is what starts the kernel and collects its output. On a typical
macOS machine the `python3` on `PATH` is a Homebrew build with no Jupyter in it,
and `quarto render` then fails on a document whose kernel is installed and
working:

```
ERROR: Jupyter kernel 'php' not found. Known kernels: python3
```

The install block asks that interpreter for `jupyter_client` before anything
else and names it in `--python` when it has it, so Quarto and the kernelspec
agree on one Python and nothing needs overriding. When it has no Jupyter, the
block builds a virtual environment and puts it first on `PATH`, where Quarto
finds it as `python3`.

`quarto check jupyter` reports the interpreter Quarto chose, whether it has
Jupyter, and the kernels it can see through it:

```
Path: /Users/you/.venvs/juphyter/bin/python
Jupyter: 5.9.1
Kernels: php, python3
```

A `Jupyter: (None)` line there is this failure, whatever `jupyter kernelspec
list` reports. The kernel is not the problem in that case, and the kernelspec
needs no reinstall. `quarto check` writes its report to standard error, so pipe
it through `2>&1` before a `grep`.

In VS Code or Positron, the interpreter selected for the workspace is the one
Quarto receives, so an error that survives an otherwise correct install usually
means that selection names an interpreter with no Jupyter in it.

`QUARTO_PYTHON` names an interpreter outright, for one shell or one project.
Quarto reads it from the environment first, then from a project `_environment`
file beside `_quarto.yml`, and falls back to the first `python3` on `PATH`. The
file cannot override a variable the environment already carries, which is what
makes the editor's selection decisive: the Quarto extension sets
`QUARTO_PYTHON` from it on every render, so a wrong selection is corrected
through the interpreter picker and not through a file.

Exporting it from a shell startup file is worth avoiding, because it takes
precedence over an activated virtual environment and would therefore change the
interpreter for every Quarto project on the machine.

### When no Python can host the kernel

The kernelspec names an interpreter with `ipykernel` 7 or newer, and a machine
whose only Python is the system or a Homebrew build has none. Those builds are
marked externally managed, so `pip install` into them refuses, which leaves a
virtual environment as the supported way out.

`juphyter install` offers to build one when it finds no interpreter that works:

```
Build a virtual environment with jupyterlab at /Users/you/.venvs/juphyter and
install the kernel into it? [y/N]
```

`--create-venv PATH` answers that in advance, which is what a script or a CI
job needs:

```bash
juphyter install --create-venv ~/.venvs/juphyter
```

The environment gets `jupyterlab`, which carries the `ipykernel` the kernelspec
names and the `jupyter_client` that Quarto starts a kernel through, so one
environment answers both. An environment already at that path is adopted rather
than rebuilt, and the packages are installed either way, so a second run
finishes an interrupted one. A directory that exists and holds something else is
refused rather than written into.

Pointing Quarto at the environment is still yours to do, and the command prints
how. With no terminal to put the question to, the environment is built without
asking: there is nobody there to answer, and it is written under your home
directory without touching any interpreter that was already on the machine.

An explicit `--python` turns the offer off. Naming an interpreter is a decision
about which one to use, and building a different one would answer a question you
did not ask.

### Pointing Quarto at the environment

A new environment is of no use to Quarto until Quarto runs it. In Positron, VS
Code, or Cursor, select it for the workspace with **Python: Select
Interpreter**. The Quarto extension hands the workspace interpreter to Quarto
for every render in that workspace, so no other project changes.

At a terminal, activate it for the shell:

```bash
source ~/.venvs/juphyter/bin/activate
```

juphyter writes nothing to a shell startup file. An entry in one would change
`python3` for every Quarto project on the machine, which is the harm that keeps
`QUARTO_PYTHON` out of a startup file as well.

## Checking an install later

`juphyter install` reports what it recorded at the moment it recorded it, and
everything it names can move afterwards. A `brew upgrade` replaces the PHP
binary a kernelspec points at, a deleted project takes the engine inside its
`vendor` directory, a removed virtual environment takes the interpreter, and a
new terminal can carry a `PATH` that no longer reaches the Jupyter the kernel
was installed against. Each of those leaves a kernel that a front end lists and
cannot start, and none of them changes the kernelspec.

`juphyter doctor` asks those questions and changes nothing:

```
juphyter doctor

This package
  ok    the Python wrapper is at /Users/you/.composer/vendor/.../kernel

PHP
  ok    PHP 8.5.10 at /opt/homebrew/bin/php
  ok    pcntl is there, so the stop button interrupts a cell

A Python for the kernel
  ok    /Users/you/.venvs/juphyter/bin/python has ipykernel 7.4.0

Quarto
  fail  quarto will run /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.14, which has no Jupyter

Kernels in /Users/you/Library/Jupyter/kernels
  ok    php is complete
  fail  php83: its PHP /opt/homebrew/Cellar/php/8.3.1/bin/php does not run

JupyterLab: ready, with php.
Quarto: not ready.
```

The `PATH` entry it suggests comes from an interpreter it has just confirmed
has `ipykernel`, which is a kernel's own interpreter when the one a fresh
install would pick no longer works. It is printed twice, as an `export` for the
shell you are in and as the append that keeps it, because the first alone lasts
only until that shell closes. `--prefix` looks under a prefix rather than
the per-user directory, and the exit code is 1 when anything is broken, so a
script can ask.

A kernel juphyter did not write is left out of the report, as `juphyter
uninstall` refuses to remove one.

## Your first Quarto document

Write a document in any directory, with no project around it:

````markdown
---
title: "PHP in Quarto"
jupyter: php
---

::: {#3313d2a6 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.php .cell-code}
echo "sum: ", array_sum(range(1, 10)), "\n";
PHP_VERSION;
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
sum: 55
```
:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1}
```
'8.5.10'
```
:::
:::


````

`quarto render hello.qmd` runs the cell and puts its output in the HTML. Cell
options work as they do for any other engine, because PHP accepts `#` comments.

In JupyterLab, started with `jupyter lab`, the same kernel appears in the
launcher under the PHP version it found.

## Checking it worked

```bash
juphyter doctor
```

It names what it found and says which front ends work.
[Checking an install later](#checking-an-install-later) covers the report and
what each finding means. `jupyter kernelspec list` is the narrower question of
whether Jupyter can see the kernelspec at all.

## The phpstats packages

None of them is a dependency of juphyter, which installs and runs with any
subset of the family present, including none of it. The install above therefore
runs plain PHP, and phibble tables and phiz plots need the packages added.

A second kernel gives them to a document in any directory:

```bash
for r in phibble phplyr; do
  composer global config "repositories.$r" \
    "{\"type\":\"vcs\",\"url\":\"https://github.com/phpstats/$r\",\"no-api\":true}"
done
composer global require --prefer-source "phpstats/phibble:^0.3" "phpstats/phplyr:^0.3"

juphyter install --name phpstats --display-name "PHP (phpstats)" \
  --autoload "$(composer global config home 2>/dev/null)/vendor/autoload.php"
```

Name that kernel in the front matter as `jupyter: phpstats`.

It is a second kernel rather than a change to the first because `--autoload`
fixes one autoloader for every document it runs, which suits a document outside
any project and breaks one inside a project. The `php` kernel keeps the default
search described under [Which dependencies a notebook
sees](#which-dependencies-a-notebook-sees), so a document inside a Composer
project sees that project's own packages.

The packages are not on Packagist, so each needs a `repositories` entry with
`"no-api": true`, which makes Composer read the repository with `git` rather
than through the GitHub API and so needs no token. `--prefer-source` is needed
for the same reason, because a dist zipball still comes from the API.

Use the released `^0.3` tags rather than `dev-main` for these. phplyr requires
`phpstats/phibble ^0.3`, which a `dev-main` phibble does not satisfy, so asking
for `dev-main` on both fails to resolve.

phiz requires PHP 8.5 and has to be left out below that. On 8.5 or newer, add
it with `composer global require --prefer-source "phpstats/phiz:^0.3"`.

## Inside a single project

Installing juphyter as a project dependency pins the kernel's version with the
project:

```bash
composer require --dev phpstats/juphyter
vendor/bin/juphyter install
```

The kernelspec it writes is still the machine's, and it names that project's
copy of the engine. Two consequences follow. Running the same command from a
second project replaces the first kernelspec, which `juphyter install` reports
as `Replaced`, and deleting the project's `vendor` directory leaves every
notebook on the machine pointing at an engine that is gone. Give each project's
kernel its own `--name` to keep them apart.

## Without Composer: the standalone PHAR

A standalone PHAR gives you a kernel on a machine with no Composer:

```bash
php juphyter.phar install
```

The kernelspec then names the PHAR as its engine, and the engine finds a
project's dependencies at run time by walking up from the notebook's own
directory. A PHAR install also copies the Python wrapper out of the archive and
beside the kernelspec, because Python cannot import from inside a `phar://`
path.

## Several PHP versions at once

Each kernel needs its own name, and the display name follows the version it
finds:

```bash
juphyter install --name php83 --php /path/to/php83
juphyter install --name php85 --php /path/to/php85
```

That produces two kernels in the launcher, "PHP 8.3" and "PHP 8.5". Pass
`--display-name` to label them yourself.

An absolute `--php` path is recorded as you wrote it. That matters with
Homebrew, where resolving the symlink would pin the kernelspec to a versioned
path such as `/opt/homebrew/Cellar/php/8.5.10/bin/php` that `brew upgrade`
removes. A bare name such as `php8.4` is still resolved to an absolute path,
since a kernelspec cannot rely on your `PATH`.

## Where the kernelspec goes

`juphyter install` writes to the per-user Jupyter data directory, which is
`~/Library/Jupyter/kernels` on macOS and `$XDG_DATA_HOME/jupyter/kernels` or
`~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels` on Linux. `JUPYTER_DATA_DIR` and
`JUPYTER_PLATFORM_DIRS` are both honored, as `jupyter --paths` reports them.
`--prefix PATH` writes under `PATH/share/jupyter` instead, which is the layout
`jupyter kernelspec install --prefix` produces.

`juphyter uninstall` removes a kernelspec, and only one that juphyter wrote. It
refuses to delete somebody else's kernel of the same name, as does a reinstall.

## Which dependencies a notebook sees

The engine starts in the notebook's own directory, walks up looking for
`vendor/autoload.php`, and loads the first one it finds. A notebook anywhere
inside a Composer project therefore sees that project's packages with no
configuration.

Two ways to override that search, and the most explicit one wins.
`JUPHYTER_AUTOLOAD` in the environment comes first, which is what `--autoload`
at install time records in the kernelspec. A `juphyter.json` beside the
notebook, or anywhere above it, comes second, and can set the same thing along
with two run-time settings:

```json
{
  "autoload": "vendor/autoload.php",
  "memory_limit": "512M",
  "include_path": "lib"
}
```

Relative paths in that file resolve against the file's own directory, so one
`juphyter.json` at a project's root serves every notebook beneath it.

## Static images

Plots render as interactive charts in JupyterLab and in Quarto's HTML output
with nothing else installed. Rendering a Quarto document to PDF or Word needs a
static image, which phiz produces with the
[vl-convert](https://github.com/vega/vl-convert) binary. Put it on your `PATH`,
or name it in `PHIZ_VL_CONVERT`. Without it, a plot in a PDF falls back to its
text description.

The Python package `vl-convert-python` is not a substitute: it ships a library
and no executable, and phiz runs the binary.

Either override replaces the search rather than extending it. A kernel
installed with `--autoload` loads that one autoloader for every notebook it
runs, including a notebook that sits inside a Composer project of its own, so
keep such a kernel under its own `--name` as [The phpstats
packages](#the-phpstats-packages) does.
